note: Documents that social bias can rise with scale in ambiguous contexts, a finding an audit can use to challenge the assumption that bigger models are safer.
title: Beyond the Imitation Game: Quantifying and extrapolating the capabilities of language models

reading.body:
Scale improves benchmark scores and confidence calibration but does not make models safe, and social bias can rise with size in ambiguous contexts.

BIG-bench tested 204 tasks across linguistics, math, common sense, biology, physics, and social bias, with human experts completing every task as a baseline. Scores and confidence estimates rose with parameter count across model families from millions to hundreds of billions of parameters, yet absolute performance stayed weak and below human raters. Two patterns emerged: gradual improvement on tasks that reward memorized knowledge, and sudden jumps on tasks requiring multiple steps or measured by brittle metrics. Sparse models helped, and model classes otherwise behaved similarly.

The bias result is the one that should change procurement and deployment decisions. A larger model can score better on capability tests while becoming more biased in unclear situations, so scale is not a safety argument. Prompting reduced the bias in these tests, which means the harm is at least partly a function of how the model is used rather than only how large it is.

The data does not say which specific biases grew, how large the effect was, or whether prompting fixes bias outside the benchmark. It covers one suite of 204 tasks and several model families, not every architecture or any model released after 2022. It says nothing about compute, buildings, or power, so it cannot speak to whether the grid constrains this kind of scaling.

explain_beginner: Researchers built a large test called BIG-bench to check what language models can and cannot do. It has 204 tasks from many fields, created by hundreds of people. They tested several model families and compared them with human experts. Bigger models generally scored better and judged their own confidence better, but still did poorly overall and far below people. Different model types behaved similarly, though sparse models helped. Some skills improved steadily, often when memorized knowledge mattered. Other skills appeared suddenly, often when tasks needed several steps. Social bias grew with size in unclear situations, but prompting could reduce it. This helps researchers prepare for new abilities and harmful effects.
explain_business: Executives should not treat model size as a guarantee of safety or quality. A large benchmark with 204 tasks from many fields tested several model families, from millions to hundreds of billions of parameters, against human experts. Larger models improved, but their absolute performance and confidence estimates stayed weak and below people. Different model types performed similarly, though sparse designs helped. Some abilities grew steadily from memorized knowledge, while others appeared suddenly and depended on multi-step tasks or fragile measures. Social bias increased with scale in unclear contexts, but prompting could reduce it. This informs decisions to fund evaluation, human baselines, and bias testing rather than assuming scale is enough.
explain_practitioner: Researchers assembled BIG-bench, a 204-task suite contributed by 450 authors from 132 institutions. Tasks span linguistics, child development, math, common sense, biology, physics, social bias, software. They evaluated OpenAI GPT models, Google dense transformers, and sparse transformers in the Switch style across sizes from millions to hundreds of billions of parameters. Human experts completed every task as a baseline. Results show scores and confidence estimates rise with size but stay weak and below human raters. Model classes behave similarly, with sparse models helping. Gradual, predictable improvements involve knowledge or memorization. Sudden breakthroughs involve multiple steps, components, or brittle metrics. Social bias rises with scale in ambiguous contexts, though prompting helps.
